common_name: Piel de Sapo Melon (Spanish Toad-Skin Winter Melon)
scientific_name: Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Piel de Sapo'

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the soil is thoroughly warm; Piel de Sapo needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten, making it a strong fit for the extended Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis with slings to support the heavy fruit. Piel de Sapo, meaning 'toad skin' in Spanish, is a classic Spanish winter melon named for its distinctive mottled dark and pale green rind, an oblong fruit that hides sweet, crisp, pale green-white flesh with a mild, delicate flavor. Unlike musky cantaloupe types, this inodorus-group melon develops little to no aroma at the stem even when fully ripe, so growers judge readiness by days from planting, a slight softening at the blossom end, and a duller rind color rather than by scent, and the fruit also stores notably longer after harvest than most melons. Water deeply but infrequently once fruit begins sizing up, and reduce watering in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sugars.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed thoroughly; give vines full sun and room to sprawl or a sturdy trellis with fruit slings.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to the strongest seedlings once established. Amish Melon is an open-pollinated heirloom muskmelon preserved and passed down through generations of Amish farming families, producing medium to large, netted, orange-fleshed cantaloupe-type fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor typical of well-grown heirloom melons. The vigorous, productive vines are known for reliable fruit set and good flavor even in less-than-ideal seasons, a hallmark of many Amish-preserved garden varieties bred for dependable performance in working farm gardens rather than showy uniformity. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind color has turned from green to tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness.

common_name: Grand Rapids Lettuce (Historic American Loose-Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in fall; fast-growing and reasonably heat tolerant for a leaf lettuce, making it a good choice for stretching the Gulf Coast lettuce season.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Grand Rapids is a historic American loose-leaf lettuce introduced in the late 1800s that became the standard commercial greenhouse lettuce variety across the United States for much of the early 20th century, prized for its light green, deeply frilled, crinkled leaves and fast, dependable growth. It does not form a true head, instead producing a loose rosette that can be harvested leaf by leaf for a cut-and-come-again crop or cut whole at the base once full size is reached. Grand Rapids is more heat- and cold-tolerant than many lettuce varieties, extending the usable harvest window on either end of the cool season, though very hot weather will still eventually push it to bolt and turn bitter.

common_name: Merlot Lettuce (Deep Burgundy Frilled Loose-Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in fall for a second crop; the deep burgundy color intensifies with cooler temperatures and higher light, making fall plantings especially vivid.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Merlot is a loose-leaf lettuce grown as much for its striking appearance as for eating, producing deeply ruffled, glossy leaves in one of the darkest, most saturated wine-red colors available in lettuce, deepening further with cool nights and bright light. The flavor is sweet and mild despite the intense color, and the ruffled texture and dramatic hue make it a standout addition to salad mixes and a popular choice for edible landscaping in ornamental beds and containers. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole loose head once it reaches full size; like most leaf lettuces it bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plan plantings for the cooler shoulder seasons.
